reading.rtitle: Nurses in the Spotlight: Day Two at the Robotic Surgery Summit
paras: Day two of the Robotic Surgery Summit in Mexico City opened with a plenary on one simple question: how can a hospital keep a robotic program alive after the first year? Ken Walsh, who chaired the session, reminded the audience that buying a robot is the easy part. 'The hard part,' he said, 'is building a team that still works well in year five.'

The most popular breakout session of the day was about nursing teams. A panel of nurses from Brazil, Chile and Mexico showcased what their teams had learned. When their programs started, most of them had never worked with a robot before. In hindsight, they agreed, the first fifty cases were the most important: that is when a team builds its habits, good or bad.

One insight came up again and again. Although every hospital is different, it seems that the same three things make a program sustainable: a fixed team, regular training on the simulator, and simple benchmarks, such as setup time, that everybody can see. One team from Sao Paulo cut its setup time from more than forty minutes to about twenty-two, and the panel said that data like this helps to keep the momentum when the excitement of the first cases is gone.

Not everything is easy, of course. Several speakers said they would like to scale up to more hospitals, but only as long as each new center trains its nurses before the first case. 'Growth pays off,' one panelist said, 'provided that you do not grow faster than your team.' The summit closes tomorrow with a plenary on the future of robotic nursing in Latin America.
reading.source: Summit Daily -- a fictional newsletter written for this simulation (the summit, the people and the numbers are not real)

listenings.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the closing plenary of the Robotic Surgery Summit. My name is Ken Walsh, and I'm chairing this last session. Before we start, a little housekeeping. Each speaker has five minutes for a final reflection, and after that, we'll take questions from the floor. Our first speaker is a nurse from Einstein Hospital in Sao Paulo. Three years ago, her team had never worked with a robot. Today, their setup time is about half of what it was, and two other centers in Brazil are collecting the same data. She is going to share what she learned, in hindsight, and what comes next. Please welcome Andreia Heins.

Thank you, Ken. When I first stood at a podium in English, I had prepared every word, and I was still very nervous. In hindsight, the problem was not my English. I was trying to be perfect, not clear. So here is my insight from this summit. A robotic program does not grow because of the robot. It grows when the team keeps the momentum, year after year. Although our results are good, it seems that the real work starts now. Next year, we would like to scale up to two more hospitals, provided that their nurses train with our team first. And on a personal note, today I gave this whole talk in English, and I felt like myself. Thank you.
